[[Right-wing populism|right-wing populist]] [[political party in New Zealand]], founded and led by [[Winston Peters]], who has served three times as [[Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand|deputy prime minister]]. The party has participated in [[coalition government]]s with the [[New Zealand National Party]] from 1996 to 1998 and from 2023 to the present, and with the [[New Zealand Labour Party]] from 2017 to 2020. From 2005 to 2008, it supported a Labour-led government through a confidence-and-supply agreement. New Zealand First currently serves in a coalition government with both National and [[ACT New Zealand]] as part of the [[Sixth National Government of New Zealand|Sixth National government]], having won 6.08% of the total party vote in the [[2023 New Zealand general election]]. New Zealand First was formed shortly before the [[1993 New Zealand general election]], following the resignation of Winston Peters as the National Party MP for [[Tauranga]] after criticising the party's [[Neoliberalism|neoliberal]] [[Ruthanasia|economic policies]].{{Cite news |last=Cooke |first=Henry |date=26 September 2023 |title=How a politician most people won't vote for could shape the New Zealand government |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/sep/27/how-a-politician-most-people-wont-vote-for-could-shape-the-new-zealand-government |access-date=10 March 2024 |work=[[The Guardian]] |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}} The party gained support from National Party and Labour voters alike disenchanted with the support of both parties for extensive [[deregulation]]. New Zealand First entered the [[New Zealand House of Representatives]] shortly after its formation. The party had 17 [[members of parliament]] (MPs) at its peak, following the [[1996 New Zealand general election]], the first to use [[mixed-member proportional representation]]. That election the party swept the [[Māori electorates|Māori seats]], leading to the "[[Tight Five]]" of New Zealand First MPs from those electorates. The party had gained considerable support among socially conservative [[Māori politics#Māori in mainstream parties|Māori voters]],Jonathan Boston, Stephen Levine, Elizabeth McLeay, Nigel S. Roberts, ''The 1996 General Election in New Zealand: Proportional Representation and Political Change'', The Australian Quarterly, Vol. 69, No. 1 (Autumn, 1997), pp.9–14{{Cite news |title=What's changed? From Winston's somewhat woke-looking 1996 coalition agreement to today |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/133242570/whats-changed-from-winstons-somewhat-wokelooking-1996-coalition-agreement-to-today |last=Witton |first=Bridie |date=11 November 2023 |access-date=10 March 2024 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]}}Durie, Mason. (1998) ''Te Mana Te Kawanatanga: The Politics of Maori Self-determination''. Oxford University Press, Auckland, 103 an association still visible today.{{cite journal|last=Donovan|first=Todd|title=Misclassifying Parties as Radical Right / Right Wing Populist: A Comparative Analysis of New Zealand First|journal=Political Science|volume=72|issue=1|year=2020|pages=58–76|doi=10.1080/00323187.2020.1855992}}{{Cite web |last=Gifford |first=Adam |date=26 November 2023 |title=Māori conservatism factor on new Cabinet |url=https://waateanews.com/2023/11/27/maori-conservatism-factor-on-new-cabinet/ |access-date=10 March 2024 |website=Waatea News: Māori Radio Station |language=en-NZ}} By the end of their first term, however, the New Zealand First caucus had fallen to nine MPs due to [[Mauri Pacific|internal conflict]] over the coalition government with the National Party. After agreeing a [[confidence and supply]] with Labour in [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005]], the party left parliament following the [[2008 New Zealand general election]] in which it failed to gain enough [[party vote]]s to retain seats. However, in the [[2011 New Zealand general election]], New Zealand First gained 6.59% of the total party vote, entitling it to eight MPs. The party increased its number of MPs to eleven at the [[2014 New Zealand general election]]. During the [[2017 New Zealand general election|2017 election]], the party's number of MPs dropped to nine members.{{cite web |title=2017 General Election – Official Result |url=http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171007120051/http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/ |archive-date=7 October 2017 |access-date=7 October 2017 |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|New Zealand Electoral Commission]]}} In the weeks following the 2017 election, New Zealand First formed a [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|coalition government with the Labour Party]].{{cite news |date=24 October 2017 |title=Coalition agreement NZ First and Labour |url=http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA1710/S00058/coalition-agreement-nz-first-and-labour.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171027103100/http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA1710/S00058/coalition-agreement-nz-first-and-labour.htm |archive-date=27 October 2017 |access-date=1 November 2017 |publisher=[[New Zealand Labour Party]] |agency=[[Scoop (website)|Scoop]]}} In the [[2020 New Zealand general election|2020 election]] New Zealand First's share of the party vote fell to 2.6%, with all incumbent MPs, including Peters, losing their seats in Parliament. The party returned to parliament in 2023. New Zealand First distinguishes itself from the mainstream [[political establishment]] through its use of [[populism in New Zealand|populist rhetoric]], and supports binding [[referendums in New Zealand|referendums]] on major social and political issues. They are also the only party since the introduction of MMP to have formed governments with both National and Labour. ==History== ===Foundation=== [[File:WinstonPetersEuropa.jpg|thumb|[[Winston Peters]] founded the party in 1993]] In June 1992, Winston Peters, a former [[Minister of Māori Affairs]] in the [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] government of [[Jim Bolger]], was told that he would not be allowed to run for another term as National Party Member of Parliament for [[Tauranga (New Zealand electorate)|Tauranga]] in the [[1993 New Zealand general election|1993 election]].{{cite news|last1=Gulliver|first1=Aimee|title=Timeline: Winston Peters and Northland|url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/66748067/timeline-winston-peters-and-northland|access-date=16 June 2017|publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]]|archive-date=8 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170908022937/http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/66748067/timeline-winston-peters-and-northland|url-status=live}}{{cite news |title=NZ Party Moves To Expel Peters|first=David|last=Barber|work=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]|page=13|date=12 June 1992}} Peters had previously been dismissed from the Cabinet in 1991, after he publicly criticised National's economic policy, colloquially dubbed [[Ruthanasia]]. Spearheaded by Minister of Finance [[Ruth Richardson]], National arguably had gone beyond the [[Rogernomics|extensive deregulation]] started by the [[New Zealand Labour Party]] in the 1980s, enacting widespread austerity and slashing benefits in the [[Mother of all Budgets|Mother of All Budgets]] of 1991. The budget cut spending on many of the [[welfare state]] institutions established in the 1930s by the [[First Labour Government of New Zealand|First Labour Government]]. The unemployment benefit was cut by $14.00 a week, sickness benefit by $27.04, families benefit by $25.00 to $27.00 and universal payments for family benefits were completely abolished.{{cite web |last1=Russell |first1=Marcia |last2=Carlaw |first2=John |date=1996 |title=Revolution (part four) |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MsvmVKqkX_o |accessdate=4 February 2017 |website=YouTube |format=video |ref=Revpt4 |location=14:44–15:18}} After the death of protectionist former Prime Minister [[Robert Muldoon]] – who resigned from his [[Tāmaki (New Zealand electorate)|Tamaki]] constituency in protest – Peters became Ruthanasia's leading opponents, and National's most prominent dissenter. By late 1991, the National Party had become the most unpopular governing party since the [[Great Depression]], with one poll result putting them [[Opinion polling for the 1993 New Zealand general election|as low as 22%]]. After his sacking, Peters decided to capitalise on National's unpopularity.{{Cite web |title=NZ Polled |url=https://www.polled.co.nz/historicalpollingdata.php |access-date=5 May 2024 |website=www.polled.co.nz |language=en}} On 19 March 1993, Peters resigned from the National Party.{{cite news |title=NZ set for November poll. Economic recovery under way, says Bolger |first=David |last=Barber|work=[[The Age]]|page=6|date=15 September 1993}} He also resigned from Parliament, triggering [[1993 Tauranga by-election|a by-election in his electorate]] on 17 April 1993 in which he stood as an [[independent politician|independent]], winning with 90.8% of votes due to neither [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]] nor National running a candidate.{{cite web|title=Rt Hon Winston Peters|url=http://www.nzfirst.org.nz/winston_peters|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170309001124/http://www.nzfirst.org.nz/winston_peters|url-status=usurped|archive-date=9 March 2017|publisher=New Zealand First|access-date=16 June 2017|language=en}} On 18 July 1993, shortly before [[dropping the writ|the writs were issued]] for [[1993 New Zealand general election|that year's general election]], Peters formed New Zealand First as a political grouping.{{cite news |title=NZ set for November poll. Economic recovery under way, says Bolger |first=David |last=Barber|work=[[The Age]]|page=9|date=15 September 1993}} At the time of its formation, New Zealand First's policy platform was broadly [[Conservatism|conservative]] and [[reactionary]] in that it opposed both [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]] and National, the major [[Centre-left politics|centre-left]] and [[Centre-right politics|centre-right]] parties respectively. Peters claimed to be reviving National policies from which the [[Fourth National Government of New Zealand|Bolger government]] had departed. Variably dubbed a [[Social conservatism|social conservative]], [[Economic nationalism|economic nationalist]], or [[Right-wing populism|right-wing populist]],{{Cite news |last=Cooke |first=Henry |date=26 September 2023 |title=How a politician most people won't vote for could shape the New Zealand government |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/sep/27/how-a-politician-most-people-wont-vote-for-could-shape-the-new-zealand-government |access-date=8 April 2024 |work=[[The Guardian]] |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}} Peters' rise was fuelled by the enormous financial changes New Zealand underwent during the 1980s and 90s, during which time the economy was thoroughly [[Deregulation|deregulated]] by both the Labour Party and the National Party. A fierce opponent of both [[neoliberalism]] and [[progressivism]], Peters gained support from both National Party and Labour voters disenchanted with the support of both parties for [[Economic liberalization|economic liberalisation]].''Frontline'', TVNZ 1, 27 October 1993. Link – https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t9KqjmvaTu4&t=1091s As Peters was a [[Māori politics|Māori conservative]],{{cite web | last1=Gifford | first1=Adam | url=https://waateanews.com/2023/11/27/maori-conservatism-factor-on-new-cabinet/ | title=Māori conservatism factor on new Cabinet | date=26 November 2023}}{{cite web | url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/133242570/whats-changed-from-winstons-somewhat-wokelooking-1996-coalition-agreement-to-today | title=What's changed? From Winston's somewhat woke-looking 1996 coalition agreement to today}} he gained strong support particularly from socially conservative [[Māori people|Māori]] voters who had voted Labour consistently until they began enforcing neoliberal policies, colloquially called [[Rogernomics]]. The party was soon widely regarded as having a distinct Māori character or even being "pro-Māori". ===1993 general election=== [[File:New Zealand First logo.png|thumb|Original party logo (1993–2017)]] In the April 1993 [[1993 Tauranga by-election|special by-election]], [[Tauranga (New Zealand electorate)|Tauranga]] voters re-elected Peters as an independent. At the general election six months later, New Zealand First received 8.4% of the total vote.{{cite web |url=http://www.elections.org.nz/events/past-events/general-elections-1890-1993 |title=GENERAL ELECTIONS 1890–1993 |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |date=30 August 2016 |access-date=10 April 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151230122414/http://www.elections.org.nz/events/past-events/general-elections-1890-1993 |archive-date=30 December 2015 |url-status=dead}} Peters easily retained [[Tauranga (New Zealand electorate)|Tauranga]], and [[Tau Henare]], another New Zealand First candidate, won the [[Northern Maori|Northern Māori]] seat, giving the party a total of two MPs. This did much to counter the perception of New Zealand First as merely a personality-driven vehicle for Peters. ===1996 general election=== With the switch to the [[mixed-member proportional]] (MMP) electoral system for the [[1996 New Zealand general election|1996 election]], smaller parties could gain a share of seats proportional to their share of the vote. Before the election, New Zealand First was polling unprecedentedly highly due to the popularity of its leader, Winston Peters. At its peak, New Zealand First was polling at 29% support on 16 May 1996.{{Cite web |title=NZ Polled |url=https://www.polled.co.nz/historicalpollingdata.php |access-date=2 October 2023 |website=www.polled.co.nz |language=en |archive-date=3 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231003045204/https://www.polled.co.nz/historicalpollingdata.php |url-status=live}} This enabled New Zealand First to win 13% of the vote and 17 seats, including all five [[Māori electorates]]. New Zealand First's five Māori MPs—[[Tau Henare]] (the party's deputy leader), [[Tuku Morgan]], [[Rana Waitai]], [[Tu Wyllie]] and [[Tuariki Delamere]]—became known as the "[[Tight Five]]".{{cite web |last1=Sullivan |first1=Ann |title=Tōrangapū – Māori and political parties – National, New Zealand First, Māori and Mana parties |url=https://teara.govt.nz/en/torangapu-maori-and-political-parties/page-4 |publisher=[[Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand]] |access-date=29 August 2019 |date=18 July 2016 |archive-date=10 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200810085050/https://teara.govt.nz/en/torangapu-maori-and-political-parties/page-4 |url-status=live}} The election result put New Zealand First in a powerful position just three years after its formation. Neither of the two traditional major parties ([[New Zealand National Party|National]] and [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]]) had enough seats to govern alone, and only New Zealand First had enough seats to become a realistic [[Coalition government|coalition]] partner for either. This placed the relatively new party in a position where it was the [[kingmaker]], a position which allowed the party to effectively choose the next [[Prime Minister of New Zealand]]. New Zealand First entered into negotiations with both major parties. Before the election, most people (including many New Zealand First voters) had expected Peters to enter into coalition with [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]]. In fact, he harshly attacked his former [[New Zealand National Party|National]] colleagues during the campaign, and appeared to promise that he would not even consider going into coalition with them.{{cite web |last1=Sachdeva |first1=Sam |title=Reading the tea leaves from 1996 |url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2017/07/29/40392/reading-the-tea-leaves-from-1996 |website=[[Newsroom (website)|Newsroom]] |access-date=30 August 2019 |language=en-AU |date=30 July 2017 |archive-date=29 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190829204026/https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2017/07/29/40392/reading-the-tea-leaves-from-1996 |url-status=live}} ===Coalition with National: 1996–1998=== To the surprise of the electorate, which had apparently voted for New Zealand First to get rid of National, New Zealand First decided to enter a coalition ''with'' National, enabling and becoming part of the third term of the [[Fourth National Government of New Zealand|fourth National government]]. The most common explanation for this decision involved National's willingness to accept New Zealand First's demands (and/or Labour's refusal to do so). However, [[Michael Laws]] (a former National Party MP who served as a New Zealand First campaign manager) claims that Peters had secretly decided to go with National significantly before this time, and that he merely used negotiations with Labour to encourage more concessions from National.{{cite book |last1=Easton |first1=Brian |title=The Whimpering of the State: Policy After MMP |date=1 October 2013 |publisher=Auckland University Press |isbn=978-1-86940-796-4 |page=61 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n-paAwAAQBAJ&pg=PT61 |language=en}} Whatever the case, New Zealand First exacted a high price from Bolger in return for allowing him to stay in power. Under the terms of a detailed coalition agreement, Peters would serve as [[Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand|Deputy Prime Minister]], and would also hold the specially created office of [[Treasurer]] (senior to the [[Minister of Finance (New Zealand)|Minister of Finance]]). National also made considerable concessions on policy. Unusually for a junior coalition partner in a Westminster system (especially one as new as New Zealand First), Peters was free to select the ministers from his own party, without Bolger's oversight.{{cite book |last1=Hazan |first1=Reuven Y. |last2=Longley |first2=Lawrence D. |title=The Uneasy Relationships Between Parliamentary Members and Leaders |date=4 April 2014 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-26838-1 |page=129 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=X_5HAwAAQBAJ |language=en |access-date=22 March 2023 |archive-date=13 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230513155044/https://books.google.com/books?id=X_5HAwAAQBAJ |url-status=live}} New Zealand First had a relatively smooth coalition relationship with National at first. Despite early concerns about the ability of Peters to work with Bolger, who had sacked him from cabinet during his time as [[Minister for Māori Development|Minister of Māori Affairs]] in 1991, the two did not have major problems. New Zealand First had graver concerns about the behaviour of some of its MPs. A particularly damaging scandal involved [[Tuku Morgan]], which consisted of him allegedly spending $4000 in public funds on clothing,{{Cite web |date=31 January 2009 |title=Mallard tries to stay afloat |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/sunday-news/latest-edition/38376/Mallard-tries-to-stay-afloat |access-date=30 September 2023 |website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en |archive-date=2 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231002144700/https://www.stuff.co.nz/sunday-news/latest-edition/38376/Mallard-tries-to-stay-afloat |url-status=live}} though the [[Serious Fraud Office (New Zealand)|Serious Fraud Office]] later did not find him guilty of [[fraud]].{{Cite web |date=1 October 2023 |title='Close eye' on TV grant to Tuku Morgan |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/close-eye-on-tv-grant-to-tuku-morgan/UOT77XND6WHFSIL3N3FJOXNPUE/ |access-date=30 September 2023 |website=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |language=en-NZ |archive-date=2 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231002144702/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/close-eye-on-tv-grant-to-tuku-morgan/UOT77XND6WHFSIL3N3FJOXNPUE/ |url-status=live}} Gradually, however, the coalition tensions became more significant than problems of party discipline. This became increasingly the case after [[Ministry of Transport (New Zealand)|Transport Minister]] [[Jenny Shipley]] gained enough support within the National party room to force Bolger's resignation{{Cite web |date=27 April 2017 |title=The Challenger – Jenny Shipley |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/programmes/the-9th-floor/story/201841731/the-challenger-jenny-shipley |access-date=30 September 2023 |website=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz |archive-date=2 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231002144658/https://www.rnz.co.nz/programmes/the-9th-floor/story/201841731/the-challenger-jenny-shipley |url-status=live}} and to subsequently become New Zealand's first woman Prime Minister on 8 December 1997. The tensions between the two parties also rose as New Zealand First adopted a more aggressive approach to promoting its policies (including those National would not implement). This new attitude probably fed off New Zealand First's poor performance in [[Opinion polling for the 1999 New Zealand general election|opinion polls]], which (to Peters) indicated that the party's success rested on its confrontational style. Many commentators believe that Peters performs better in [[Parliamentary opposition|opposition]] than in government. ===Return to opposition=== On 14 August 1998, Shipley sacked Peters from [[Cabinet of New Zealand|Cabinet]]. This occurred after an ongoing dispute about the sale of the government's stake in [[Wellington Airport|Wellington International Airport]],{{cite news |date=29 August 2007 |title=Once, twice, three times a break-up |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=10529769 |access-date=2 May 2018 |archive-date=26 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180626084742/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=10529769 |url-status=live}} directly in conflict with New Zealand First's general commitment to not sell off state assets. Peters immediately tore up the coalition agreement. However, several other MPs, unwilling to follow Peters into opposition and wanting to continue to support a National-led government, tried to replace Peters as Leader of New Zealand First with [[Tau Henare]], the then-Deputy Leader. This caucus-room coup failed, and Henare eventually led four other New Zealand First MPs in forming a new party, [[Mauri Pacific]], which was a self-proclaimed [[Multiculturalism|multicultural]] party. Three others established themselves as [[Independent politician|independents]]. All eight departing MPs continued to support a National-led [[minority government]]. Many of these MPs had come under public scrutiny for their behaviour.{{Citation needed|date=October 2023}} Until the dissolution of [[New Zealand Parliament|Parliament]] in 1999, they provided Shipley with enough parliamentary support to stay in government without New Zealand First.{{cite news |title=NZ's greatest waka-jumpers of all time |url=https://www.odt.co.nz/opinion/nzs-greatest-waka-jumpers-all-time |access-date=9 June 2022 |work=[[Otago Daily Times]] |date=2 March 2018 |language=en |archive-date=8 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220808221211/https://www.odt.co.nz/opinion/nzs-greatest-waka-jumpers-all-time |url-status=live }} ===1999 general election=== In the [[1999 New Zealand general election|1999 election]] New Zealand First lost much of its support, receiving only 4% of the party vote.{{cite web |title=Summary of Overall Results |url=http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_1999/e9/html/e9_partI.html |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |access-date=22 April 2018 |archive-date=27 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180127033932/http://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_1999/e9/html/e9_partI.html |url-status=live }} Some voters had not forgiven Peters for forming a coalition with National after being led to believe that a vote for him would help get rid of National, and others likely changed their vote due to the instability within the party's ranks. Whatever the case, New Zealand First's support tailed off enough that it was nearly ejected from parliament. Under New Zealand's MMP system, a party must either win an electorate seat or 5% of the vote to qualify for list seats. Peters held his Tauranga electorate by a mere 63 votes after losing almost 20 percent of his vote from 1996, and New Zealand First received five seats in total.{{cite web |title=Winning Electorate Candidate Votes |url=http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_1999/e9/html/e9_partVI.html |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |access-date=22 April 2018 |archive-date=27 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180127034056/http://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_1999/e9/html/e9_partVI.html |url-status=live }} ===2002 general election=== By the [[2002 New Zealand general election]], however, the party had rebuilt much of its support. This occurred largely because of Peters' three-point campaign for sensible immigration, scrutinising Treaty costs, and reducing crime.{{Citation needed|date=October 2016}} The party won 10.38% of the vote, which was a considerable improvement on its previous performance (although not as good as its performance in 1996), and New Zealand First won thirteen seats in parliament.{{cite web |title=Official Count Results – Overall Status |url=http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2002/partystatus.html |publisher=Electoral Commission |access-date=7 August 2013 |archive-date=8 February 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130208054119/http://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2002/partystatus.html |url-status=live }} Peters' campaign slogan "Can We Fix It? Yes We Can"{{cite web |last1=Cooke |first1=Henry |title=A brief history of Winston Raymond Peters |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/97547465/a-brief-history-of-winston-raymond-peters |publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |access-date=10 November 2019 |date=21 June 2018 |archive-date=26 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180626030710/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/97547465/a-brief-history-of-winston-raymond-peters |url-status=live }} attracted much media attention, as the same line appears in theme music for the children's television programme ''[[Bob the Builder]]''. Party activists stated they were unaware the chant came from a children's cartoon.{{cite news |last1=Masters |first1=Catherine |title=Peters looks on winning treble |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/peters-looks-on-winning-treble/H2QQ7ZMJTBCSOF2FRAAFNVWGWU/ |access-date=9 June 2022 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=19 July 2002 |language=en-NZ |archive-date=8 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220608200459/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/peters-looks-on-winning-treble/H2QQ7ZMJTBCSOF2FRAAFNVWGWU/ |url-status=live }} In the end, New Zealand First gained 8 seats in [[New Zealand Parliament|Parliament]] after the election, earning 13 MPs in total (including 1 electorate MP): Winston Peters, [[Peter Brown (New Zealand politician)|Peter Brown]], [[Brian Donnelly (New Zealand politician)|Brian Donnelly]], [[Ron Mark]], [[Doug Woolerton]], [[Barbara Stewart (politician)|Barbara Stewart]], [[Pita Paraone]], [[Craig McNair]], [[Jim Peters (politician)|Jim Peters]], [[Dail Jones]], [[Edwin Perry]], [[Bill Gudgeon]], and [[Brent Catchpole]]. It appears that New Zealand First had hoped to play in 2002 a similar role to the one it had in 1996, where it found itself able to give power to either Labour or National depending on which offered the best deal. However, [[New Zealand National Party|National]]'s support, under the leadership of future [[Prime Minister of New Zealand|Prime Minister]] [[Bill English]], had collapsed to its worst result in the party's history, to the extent that it could not form a government even with New Zealand First's support, depriving the party of its hoped kingmaker position. In the end, however, this proved irrelevant, as Labour refused to consider an alliance with New Zealand First in any case{{Citation needed|date=October 2023}}. Instead, Labour relied on support from the newly significant [[United Future New Zealand|United Future]]. After the 2002 election, in light of [[New Zealand National Party|National]]'s decreased strength, New Zealand First attempted to gain more prominence in [[Parliamentary opposition|Opposition]], frequently attacking the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]]-led [[Coalition government]] on a wide range of issues. Speculation has occurred on efforts to create a more united front linking New Zealand First, the [[New Zealand National Party]], and [[ACT New Zealand]], but Peters has rejected this scenario, saying that the New Zealand voters will decide what alliances are necessary. Unlike the classical-liberal [[ACT New Zealand]], which portrays itself as a natural [[Coalition government|coalition]] partner for the [[New Zealand National Party]], New Zealand First welcomed the potential for a [[coalition government]] with any parliamentary [[political party]]. For a period in early 2004 New Zealand First experienced a brief decline in the polls after [[Don Brash]] became leader of the [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]], a change which hugely revived National's fortunes after the controversial but highly popular [[Orewa Speech]]. The votes that had apparently switched to New Zealand First from National seemed to return to support [[Don Brash]], and many commentators predicted that New Zealand First would lose a number of its seats in the next election{{Citation needed|date=October 2023}}. By 2005, however, the proportions had changed again, and as the campaign for the September 2005 election got under way, New Zealand First had again reached the 10% mark in [[Opinion polling for the 2005 New Zealand general election|opinion polling for the 2005 election]]. Pre-election polls put New Zealand First ahead of the other minor parties. Some thought it likely that in the event of a [[New Zealand National Party|National]] minority or [[Plurality (voting)|plurality]], unless [[ACT New Zealand|ACT]]'s fortunes dramatically improved, Don Brash would have to form a second coalition or seek a support agreement with New Zealand First to be able to form a [[government]]. Peters promised to support the party that won the most seats, or at least abstain in [[Motion of no confidence|no-confidence motions]] against it. However, he also said he would not support any [[government]] that included the [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Greens]] within [[Cabinet of New Zealand|Cabinet]]. ===Confidence and supply with Labour: 2005–2008=== In the [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005 election]], NZF lost much of its support. Though it remained the third-largest party in the House, New Zealand First took only 5.72% of the vote, a considerable loss from 2002, and just enough to cross the [[Mixed-member proportional representation|MMP]] proportionality quota of 5%. In addition, Peters narrowly lost his previously [[safe seat|safe constituency seat]] of [[Tauranga (New Zealand electorate)|Tauranga]] by 730 votes to National's [[Bob Clarkson]], and became a [[list MP]]. New Zealand First lost six seats in [[New Zealand Parliament|Parliament]], earning 7 MPs, all elected on the [[Electoral list|party list]]: Winston Peters, Peter Brown, [[Dail Jones]], [[Ron Mark]], [[Doug Woolerton]], [[Barbara Stewart (politician)|Barbara Stewart]] and [[Pita Paraone]]. Following the [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005 election]], New Zealand First agreed to a [[confidence and supply|supply-and-confidence]] agreement with the New Zealand Labour Party (along with [[United Future]]) in return for policy concessions including the [[SuperGold Card]] and the portfolio of [[Minister of Foreign Affairs (New Zealand)|Foreign Affairs]] outside [[New Zealand Cabinet|Cabinet]] for Winston Peters. Peters becoming [[Minister of Foreign Affairs (New Zealand)|Minister of Foreign Affairs]] detected a change in his attitude since Peters' "Rotorua speech" on 7 September 2005 at a public address at the Rotorua Convention Centre had spoken of New Zealand First sitting on the [[crossbenches|cross-benches]] (and thus staying out of [[New Zealand Government|government]]) and eschewing "the baubles of office".{{Cite web |date=1 October 2023 |title=Peters' baubles get a parliamentary bashing |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/peters-baubles-get-a-parliamentary-bashing/XKT6BQWD2CAEMTKONRCYWLOZJQ/ |access-date=30 September 2023 |website=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |language=en-NZ |archive-date=2 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231002144700/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/peters-baubles-get-a-parliamentary-bashing/XKT6BQWD2CAEMTKONRCYWLOZJQ/ |url-status=live }} Peters' coalition partnership with the centre-left Labour Party was in spite of his increasingly right-wing populist rhetoric around [[Asian New Zealanders|emigration from Asia]] (which was at odds with Labour's policies).{{Cite press release |date=26 April 2005 |publisher=New Zealand First Party |title=New Zealand – The Last Asian Colony |website=Scoop News |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA0504/S00527.htm |access-date=31 March 2024}}{{Cite web |date=18 October 2005 |title=Winston Peters' memorable quotes |url=https://www.theage.com.au/world/winston-peters-memorable-quotes-20051018-ge12mh.html |access-date=31 March 2024 |website=The Age |language=en}} Peters has previously warned of an "Asian invasion" of [[Asian New Zealanders|Asian migrants]] (against the evidence suggested by statistical trends). In 2005 he called New Zealand "the last Asian colony", and referred to Asian immigration as an “imported criminal activity” that would cause "chaos" to race relations.{{Cite web |last=Donnell |first=Hayden |date=11 July 2017 |title=Revealed: Winston Peters has never had a racist approach to anything |url=https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/11-07-2017/revealed-winston-peters-has-never-had-a-racist-approach-to-anything |access-date=5 May 2024 |website=[[The Spinoff]] |language=en}} Soon after the [[2005 New Zealand general election]], Winston Peters launched a legal challenge against [[Bob Clarkson]], alleging that he had spent more than the legal limit allowed for campaign budgets during elections in New Zealand. This legal bid failed, with a majority of the judges in the case declaring that [[Bob Clarkson]] had not overspent during the campaign for the [[Tauranga (New Zealand electorate)|Tauranga]] electorate. In the [[2005 New Zealand election funding controversy|2005 election funding controversy]], the [[Office of the Controller and Auditor-General|Auditor-General]] found that all the parties in parliament except the [[New Zealand Progressive Party|Progressive Party]] had misspent parliamentary funding. New Zealand First was the only party that did not repay the misspent funding.{{cite web | title=Charity turns down NZ First's donation | url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10516988 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121020115220/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10516988 | url-status=dead |archive-date=20 October 2012| work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] | date=18 June 2008 | access-date=26 April 2009}} New Zealand First achieved many policy initiatives during this term, most notably the introduction of the SuperGold Card, a policy which was unpopular among many political leaders due to its high cost. The SuperGold Card was targeted towards seniors, and included free off-peak travel, and discounts from thousands of New Zealand businesses. months before the [[2008 New Zealand general election|2008 general election]], New Zealand First became embroiled in a dispute over donations to the party from billionaire [[Owen Glenn]], the Vela family and [[Bob Jones (businessman)|Bob Jones]]. This resulted in an investigation into party finances by the [[Serious Fraud Office (New Zealand)|Serious Fraud Office]] on 28 August 2008 and an investigation into Peters by the [[New Zealand House of Representatives committees|Privileges Committee]].{{cite news |title=Peters defiant ahead of meeting |work=[[Bay of Plenty Times]] |date=29 August 2008 |url= https://www.nzherald.co.nz/bay-of-plenty-times/news/peters-defiant-ahead-of-meeting/7XQF4NZNC3QAPC3CGBDQP2A5VI/ |access-date=18 May 2026}} On 29 August 2008 Peters stood down from his ministerial roles after significant pressure, while the investigations by the Serious Fraud Office and Privileges Committee proceeded.{{cite web |title=Peters 'hurt but calm' in stepping down |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10529612 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121020095412/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10529612 |url-status=dead |archive-date=20 October 2012|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=29 August 2008 |access-date=14 September 2008}} Although the Serious Fraud Office and the police found that Peters was not guilty of any wrongdoing, the Privileges Committee decided that Peters knowingly misled Parliament by not declaring the donation,{{Cite web |date=1 October 2023 |title=Peters describes censuring as 'useless facade' |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/peters-describes-censuring-as-useless-facade/S47RZYXRE4PGDYM6DQWXZSBSA4/ |access-date=30 September 2023 |website=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |language=en-NZ |archive-date=2 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231002144658/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/peters-describes-censuring-as-useless-facade/S47RZYXRE4PGDYM6DQWXZSBSA4/ |url-status=live }} and censured Peters, which he called a "useless facade." The whole scandal harmed New Zealand First's polling in the lead-up to the election, and is widely attributed to its defeat.{{cite news |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz-election-2008/news/article.cfm?c_id=1501799&objectid=10541195 |title=Police inquiry clears NZ First |author=Claire Trevett and Patrick Gower |date=5 November 2008 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |access-date=30 October 2011 |archive-date=28 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120328102609/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz-election-2008/news/article.cfm?c_id=1501799&objectid=10541195 |url-status=live }} During the scandal, [[Leader of the Opposition (New Zealand)|Leader of the Opposition]] [[John Key]] took the opportunity to rule out working with Peters and New Zealand First, which likely contributed further to the party's defeat. As expected, [[Prime Minister of New Zealand|Prime Minister]] [[Helen Clark]] did not rule out working with New Zealand First. On election night it was clear that Peters had not regained the [[Tauranga (New Zealand electorate)|Tauranga seat]] after his last loss of the electorate in the [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005 election]] and, with 4% of party votes, had not met the 5% threshold needed for parties to be elected without an electorate seat. In what some journalists described as a 'gracious' concession speech, Peters said that 'it's not over yet. We'll reorganise ourselves in the next few months. And we'll see what 2011 might hold for all us [sic].''{{cite news |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz-election-2008/news/article.cfm?c_id=1501799&objectid=10541945 |title=Winston Peters: Gone but never forgotten |last=Gower |first=Patrick |date=9 November 2008 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |access-date=30 October 2011 |archive-date=27 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120327065921/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz-election-2008/news/article.cfm?c_id=1501799&objectid=10541945 |url-status=live }} At a post-election meeting held to discuss the party's future in February 2009, long-serving Deputy Leader [[Peter Brown (New Zealand politician)|Peter Brown]] stepped down.{{cite news |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/1400947 |title=NZ First deputy leader resigns |date=14 February 2009 |agency=[[NZPA]] |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |access-date=30 October 2011 |archive-date=26 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121026041430/http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/1400947 |url-status=live }} ===2011 general election=== At the beginning of the election campaign New Zealand First was polling at around 2% in most major polls and was effectively written off by most political commentators. Prime Minister [[John Key]] had once again ruled out working with Peters and New Zealand First, however then [[Leader of the Opposition (New Zealand)|Leader of the Opposition]] [[Phil Goff]] had stated he was open to working with New Zealand First post-election provided they made it back into Parliament.{{Citation needed|date=October 2023}} Peters received a significant amount of media attention towards the end of the campaign at the height of the [[Tea Tape scandal]] which arose during the campaign. Peters had criticised the arrangement in the [[Epsom (New Zealand electorate)|seat of Epsom]] between National and [[ACT New Zealand|ACT]] in which National encouraged its supporters to vote for the ACT candidate for their electorate MP. He railed against National for alleged negative remarks made about the then ACT leader [[Don Brash]] and New Zealand First's elderly supporters.{{Citation needed|date=October 2023}} Peters appeared on a TVNZ minor parties leaders debate and won the debate convincingly in the subsequent text poll, with a plurality of 36% of the respondents saying Peters had won.{{cite news |last1=Vance |first1=Andrea |title=Winston Peters winner in minor party debate |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/5981643/Winston-Peters-winner-in-minor-party-debate |access-date=27 March 2022 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=16 November 2011 |language=en |archive-date=17 November 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111117231247/http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/5981643/Winston-Peters-winner-in-minor-party-debate |url-status=live }} New Zealand First won 6.6% of the party vote on election night.{{cite web|url=http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/|title=NEW ZEALAND ELECTION RESULTS|work=New Zealand Electoral Commission|access-date=10 December 2011|archive-date=29 February 2000|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000229094103/http://electionresults.govt.nz/|url-status=live}} Many political experts credit the [[Tea tape scandal]] for the re-entry of New Zealand First into Parliament; however, Peters himself credits the return to Parliament to the hard work undertaken by the Party over the three years it was not represented in Parliament. In 2012 the party sacked MP [[Brendan Horan]] after allegations he stole money from his dying mother to gamble.{{cite news | url= http://www.3news.co.nz/Horan-admits-144-TAB-calls/tabid/1607/articleID/279879/Default.aspx | work= 3 News NZ | title= Horan admits 144 TAB calls | date= 10 December 2012 | access-date= 22 April 2013 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130209055631/http://www.3news.co.nz/Horan-admits-144-TAB-calls/tabid/1607/articleID/279879/Default.aspx | archive-date= 9 February 2013 | url-status= dead }} ===2014 general election=== [[File:NZ First 2014 General Election Results by Electorate.svg|thumb|New Zealand First [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 general election]] results by electorate]] In 2012, New Zealand First stated their intent to work in coalition with parties that would buy the privatised state assets back after the [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 general election]].{{cite news|title=NZ First Committed To Buying Back State-Owned Assets {{!}} Scoop News|url=http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA1206/S00276/nz-first-committed-to-buying-back-state-owned-assets.htm|access-date=16 June 2017|publisher=scoop.co.nz|date=20 June 2012|archive-date=18 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170518165336/http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA1206/S00276/nz-first-committed-to-buying-back-state-owned-assets.htm|url-status=live}} New Zealand First entered the 2014 general election campaign without providing a clear indication as to their coalition preferences. However, Peters did raise late in the campaign the prospect of a Labour-New Zealand First coalition or confidence and supply arrangement, and express some respect for the National Party, in particular the Finance Minister [[Bill English]].[http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=1132502] 7 {{Dead link|date=June 2017}} New Zealand First increased its party vote to 8.66% at the election, which took the party's representation in Parliament to 11 seats. Peters was highly critical of the conduct of the [[Labour Party of New Zealand|Labour]] and [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Green]] parties, who he blamed for the Opposition's loss.{{Cite web |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11328808 |title = Election results 2014: Winston Peters blames Labour and Greens for ro… |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140921101943/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11328808 |archive-date=21 September 2014|url-status=dead}} In 2015 Peters contested the [[2015 Northland by-election|Northland by-election]], which was held as a result of the resignation of the incumbent [[Mike Sabin]] on 30 January 2015 amid allegations of assault. Peters won the traditionally safe National seat with a majority of 4,441 over the National candidate Mark Osborne. It was the first time a New Zealand First MP held an electorate seat since Peters lost [[Tauranga (New Zealand electorate)|Tauranga]] in 2005. The win also resulted in New Zealand First acquiring a new List MP, [[Ria Bond]], which increased the party's parliamentary representation to 12 seats. On 3 July 2015 [[Ron Mark]] was elected Deputy Leader of New Zealand First, replacing [[Tracey Martin]] who had held the post since 2013.{{cite news |last1=Jones |first1=Nicholas |title=Ron Mark new NZ First deputy leader |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11475210 |access-date=3 July 2015 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=3 July 2015 |archive-date=3 July 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150703132833/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11475210 |url-status=live }} ===2017 general election=== [[File:NZ First logo 2017.png|thumb|A Fresh Face, logo introduced in 2017]] Peters has said that he will continue on as the Leader of New Zealand First.
